title: A reference-free computational algorithm for comprehensive somatic mosaic mutation detection
text:
The overarching goal of this Tool Development Project is to adapt our RUFUS germline de novo mutation
detection software for accurate and sensitive discovery of somatic mutations. We anticipate that this
development will lead to a computational mutation detection tool that can facilitate effective and accurate
discovery of somatic mutations of all types, lengths, and allele frequencies, and thus substantially contribute to
the cataloging and understanding of healthy human somatic mosaicism.

title: Recovery of reward function in nicotine use disorder using a combination of robotics, electrophysiology, and TMS
text:
Reward‐related neural dysfunction is known to accompany chronic substance
abuse and may put substance users at higher risk of treatment dropout and drug
relapse. Using a combination robotics, neuroimaging, and non-invasive brain
stimulation methods, the proposed research seeks to develop new brain-based
interventions aimed to correct the aberrant reward processes that sustain
substance use disorders. Providing current treatment programs with a highly
effective brain-based intervention may increase substance users' success in
treatment, and thereby help reduce the major burden substance use disorders
places on the US healthcare system.

title: Studying the Role of the Microenvironment on Differentiation and Maturation of Beta Cells
text:
The study and treatment of diabetes would greatly benefit from increased understanding of how human islets
are formed. Improvements in this understanding will lead to the generation of these tissues from human stem
cells for use in diabetes cell replacement therapy and drug screening.

title: Exploiting a Novel DNA Repair Defect in Ewing Sarcoma
text:
Ewing sarcoma (EwS) is an aggressive subtype of bone and soft tissue cancers in adolescents and young
adults which is recognized as a radiosensitive and chemosensitive cancer, suggesting an underlying defect in
DNA Repair. The D’Andrea laboratory has recently demonstrated that EwS cells have an intrinsic defect in
MMEJ repair. This grant will evaluate the mechanism of this defect and the potential use of novel targeted
therapies to exploit the defect.

title: Addressing Economic Stress to Improve HIV Prevention and Care Outcomes in the United States
text:
HIV high-priority populations (HHPPs) in the United States face severe economic hardship and shoulder a
hugely disproportionate share of the burden of HIV—with prevalence as high as 44% among some
subpopulations. Although economic hardship is a core driver of HIV outcomes in the general population, how
simultaneously occurring forms of economic experience are together limiting the ability of people living with or
at risk of acquiring HIV to maintain viral suppression or seronegativity is not understood—and no HIV
economic empowerment interventions have been adapted for adult HHPPs. By conducting community-based
formative research necessary to adapt, pilot test, and refine an asset-based economic empowerment
intervention to improve HIV prevention and care outcomes among HHPPs, this study proposes to contribute
innovative and novel intervention strategies to address the impacts of economic determinants of the HIV/AIDS
epidemic.

title: Core B: Data Management and Analysis Core (DMAC)
text:
DATA MANAGEMENT AND ANALYSIS CORE (DMAC) 
The overarching goal of the Data Management and Analysis Core (DMAC) is to facilitate the data management 
sharing, integration, and analysis needs of UNC-SRP researchers to elucidate multi-factorial determinants of 
iAs-induced metabolic dysfunction/diabetes. All UNC-SRP Projects and Cores will work closely with the DMAC 
to ensure maximal impact of all data produced through UNC-SRP research. The DMAC will support the 
identification and dissemination of high impact insights surrounding metabolic disease/diabetes and iAs 
exposure, geospatial predictions of iAs exposure classification, and remediation efforts.

title: Brain and behavior correlates of prenatal cannabis exposure
text:
Cannabis use during pregnancy has increased substantially, in conjunction with legalization and decreases in
the percentage of the population who believe cannabis use is harmful. Cannabis passes through the placenta
and binds to cannabinoid receptors and can potentially alter prenatal brain development. In this prospective
study, we will monitor cannabis use in pregnant women throughout their second and third trimester and
investigate infant outcomes using brain imaging and behavioral measures that our prior work has shown to be
sensitive for detecting early manifestations of neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Reprogramming of retinoid metabolism and receptor activity in intestinal epithelial plasticity
text:
PD/PI: Sethi, Nilay S
 PROJECT NARRATIVE
The intestinal epithelium requires precise control of stem cell renewal and differentiation, and disruption of this
balance contributes to inflammatory bowel disease, mucositis, polyposis syndromes, and colorectal cancer.
Retinoic acid signaling, a nutrient-derived pathway, normally enforces differentiation, but we have discovered
that aberrant induction of RARβ and accumulation of the metabolite 4-oxo-RA instead sustain stem-like plasticity
and block lineage commitment. This project will define how RA metabolism and receptor composition are rewired
to disable differentiation, thereby identifying new therapeutic strategies to restore epithelial homeostasis across
diverse gastrointestinal diseases.

title: Leveraging the National Cancer Institute’s Cancer Center Cessation Initiative (C3I) Program to Evaluate and Transform Smoking Cessation Treatment in Cancer Care
text:
Smoking is both common among adult patients with cancer and undertreated, despite strong evidence that
quitting smoking markedly improves the health of cancer patients and survivors. Too few patients with cancer
who smoke are offered and provided effective smoking treatment by their cancer care teams. The proposed
research will identify and disseminate effective and feasible smoking treatment programs for cancer centers to
increase the rates at which cancer patients who smoke quit smoking and improve their cancer recovery.

title: Differentiating slow from rapidly progressive ADPKD by cell-specific mitochondrial and transcriptional profiles
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it focuses on identifying cell-specific mitochondrial
differences between and across cell types during autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)
progression. We anticipate that similar to other conditions where mitochondria have central roles in disease
pathogenesis, the proposed studies will identify contributions of mitochondrial dysfunction and transcriptional
diversity to disease initiation and progression. These advances have the potential to transform the
development of precision-targeted therapeutics and biomarkers for monitoring ADPKD, drug selection, and
drug dosage; all unmet clinical ADPKD needs relevant to NIH’s mission of improving human health.

title: Deciphering a Novel Mechanism for Iron-sensing at Mitochondria and Its Role in Erythropoiesis
text:
Iron is an important factor for hemoglobin synthesis in red blood cells. An insufficient supply of iron is
associated with anemia. This proposal seeks to understand the molecular basis of how hemoglobin synthesis
is regulated by a mitochondrial protein-dependent signaling in iron-deficient red blood cells.

title: Transcriptional co-activator PGC-1α promotes anti-tumor immunity in colorectal cancer
text:
(2-3 sentences, lay language)
Colorectal cancer, which is the second deadliest cancer in the United States and worldwide, often does not
respond well to treatments like radiotherapy or immunotherapy, leading to poor outcomes. Our research has
shown that the transcriptional co-activator PGC-1α is almost always downregulated in human colorectal cancer
tumors, and that PGC-1α improves
radiotherapy’s ability to enhance
the visibility and sensitivity of tumors to the
immune system. We will use a novel and, in parallel, an established mouse model of colorectal cancer to test if
and how increasing PGC-1α expression in cancer cells reduces tumor growth and improves survival in synergy
with
radiotherapy and
immunotherapy.

title: Bioengineering approaches to map mechanotransduction in the living cell
text:
Relevance
How force regulates pluripotent stem cell differentiation and cell fate at the level of chromatin remains largely
elusive. We plan to determine and elucidate if and how chromatin deformation regulates pluripotent stem cell
differentiation in this project and determine the fundamental differences between normal stem cells and cancer
stem cells. The long-term goal is to develop novel approaches and strategies to intervene pathological processes
like malignant tumors.

title: Cell-directed gene therapy for pain recovery after surgery and inflammation
text:
The development of non-narcotic (non-opioid) therapeutics is urgently needed in light of the current opioid
epidemic. Pain that results from surgeries or from arthritis is linked to prolonged inflammation and is typically
treated with opiates, which places million of patients with these conditions at higher risks for opioid abuse
problems. The proposed studies will validate a specific target to promote a faster resolution of inflammation as
a new non-narcotic therapeutic strategy that has the potential to prevent or treat surgical or inflammatory pain.

title: Advanced quantitative analyses of long-read RNA-seq at the bulk and single-cell dimensions
text:
PROJECT NARRATIVE / PUBLIC HEALTH RELEVANCE STATEMENT
To fully utilize the rapidly improving long-read sequencing, we propose to develop innovative bioinformatics
software for advanced quantitative analyses of transcriptome beyond the existing focus on qualitative
analyses. We will also carry out extensive benchmarking as well as data science study to establish a guideline
of data collection and analysis for the community to use the techniques and data in a rigorous and optimal way.
In particular, we will focus on the comparative expression analyses and single-cell analyses of long-read RNA-
seq at the gene isoform level so that we can find the subtle but meaningful difference of isoform expression
that were masked by the previous studies at the gene level but were extensively suggested by the fruitful
studies of alternative splicing in a wide spectrum of biomedical contexts.

title: Structural and Functional Studies of HER Receptors
text:
Receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) are the second largest family of membrane receptors in the human genome,
responsible for transmitting signals that regulate cellular growth, proliferation, and survival. Their activation by
extracellular growth factors triggers a series of intricate and poorly understood conformational changes to relay
signals across the plasma membrane. By resolving the first high-resolution, full-length structures of human
epidermal growth factor receptors (EGFR/HERs), we aim to uncover the mechanisms underlying RTK signal
transduction, paving the way for new therapeutic strategies to address aberrant signaling in cancer and other
human diseases.

title: Multi-organ metastatic breast cancer cell-based assay platform that models organotropic metastases using patient organoids in human tissue-derived ECMs to accelerate anti-metastatic drug development
text:
In this SBIR Fast Track project, Xylyx proposes to develop and commercialize a multi-organ metastatic breast
cancer cell-based assay platform that helps scientists develop effective drugs for treating metastatic breast
cancer, the second leading cause of death from cancer. Predictive models for testing metastatic breast cancer
drugs are lacking, leaving a significant unmet need and market gap for a physiologically-relevant assay platform.
The commercial product from this project will be an assay platform that accelerates therapeutic development for
metastatic breast cancer, and empowers high-impact discoveries that will improve treatment options and
outcomes for the millions of patients with metastatic disease.

title: Quantitative in-vivo and clinical imaging (Boppart)
text: It is essential that technological advances in imaging developed in the laboratory find direct translational paths to rapidly demonstrate their clinical utility in patients, and establish the potential for improving detection, diagnosis, and monitoring of disease. While label-based optical imaging modalities have demonstrated potential in intraoperative cancer detection, mapping the microvasculature, and site-specifically targeting of altered metabolism and pathology, to name a few, these approaches often come at a significant time and financial cost due to the associated safety risks and lengthy review processes required for FDA approval of any new contrast agent or probe. Importantly, any new targeted contrast agent or probe inevitably will have some degree of non- specific binding or off-target labeling, as well as a variable degree of uptake or labeling of the targeted cell or site. In the end, the measured or imaged signal levels are always questioned. Is the signal low because the targeted pathology is minimal, or because the targeted efficiency of labeling is low? The importance of label-free imaging is therefore high, and the need for label-free imaging across size scales is great. By identifying robust label-free signals or biomarkers that indicate changes in structure, molecular composition, metabolism, and function, quantitative clinical and in vivo imaging not only becomes a feasible alternative to label-based methods, but also provides a direct and rapid translational path to clinical human studies, since regulatory approval is not additionally needed for a contrast agent or probe. This enables rapid in vivo first-to-human and limited-scale human subjects research studies (and subsequently larger clinical trials) to be performed with the new optical imaging technologies, and make early determination of the clinical utility of the technologies and the new optical biomarkers that they generate. This TRD focuses on the technological development through four specific aims that progress from 1) the sub-cellular and cellular scale, identifying optical biomarkers and signatures that would indicate more systemic disease processes, to 2) tissue sections in an advanced digital pathology platform with artificial intelligence, to 3) computational optical imaging algorithms that extend the depth and performance of optical imaging in thick tissues, and finally to 4) engineered beam delivery systems to widely expand tissue access and application for these label-free optical imaging modalities. Collectively, this project will demonstrate novel technological advances that will find a myriad of applications to advance the biological and medicine sciences, and improve diagnostic and monitoring capabilities in clinical medicine.

title: Neural Mechanisms of Depressive Symptoms in Youth with Autism SpectrumDisorder
text:
While autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is common and impairing, our lack of knowledge about the
mechanisms underlying co-occurring depression in people with ASD hinders clinical care and effective
treatments. This K23 seeks to address this gap, defining brain mechanisms associated with depressive
symptoms in adolescents with ASD compared to controls, leveraging multimodal imaging methods (resting-
state functional magnetic resonance imaging, diffusion spectrum imaging, and myelin imaging). This work is
significant because it will create the foundation for future studies defining how the brain mechanisms of co-
occurring depressive disorders in individuals with ASD change across development, and, ultimately, to develop
novel brain-targeted treatments for depression in people with ASD.

title: Evidence-Based Targets for Continuous Glucose Monitoring Metrics in Adults with Type 1 Diabetes
text: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has been shown to improve glycemic control and reduce hypoglycemia in people with type 1 diabetes (T1D). However, current recommendations for specific CGM metric targets are based on expert opinion rather than empirical evidence. Rather than relying on expert opinion, this proposal aims to fill a crucial gap in knowledge by empirically identifying evidence-based CGM metric targets that are associated with the lowest risk of diabetes complications among adults with T1D in real-world clinical practice.
